```{r libraries, include=FALSE}
library(maftools)    # summarize, visualize and compare somatic mutations (MAF files)
library(tidyverse)   # loaded after maftools so dplyr verbs are not masked
library(DT)          # interactive downloadable tables
library(knitr)       # kable for simple inline tables
```

# From Module 1

Module 1 turned the reads of **one** person into a list of **germline** variants: the ones inherited from the parents and present in every cell. Cancer adds a second layer: **somatic** mutations, acquired by the tumor cells during life and absent from the rest of the body.

To find them, a tumor exome is sequenced together with a **normal** sample of the same patient (usually blood), and a somatic caller keeps the variants present in the tumor but **not** in the normal. This module starts *after* that step, from the results of the GDC somatic pipeline for the Wilms tumors of the **TARGET** program.

**Plan:** the MAF format → one sample per patient → cohort summary → mutation burden → the genes → TP53 in detail → Favorable vs Unfavorable histology.

# Part 1 — The MAF Format

Somatic mutations of a cohort are usually shared as a **MAF** (Mutation Annotation Format) file: a table with one row per mutation, already annotated with gene, consequence and protein change. `data/somatic/` contains, built by `data-prep/build_somatic_data.R` from the GDC Data Portal:

- `TARGET_WT_somatic_mutations.maf.gz`: every open-access somatic mutation from **whole-exome sequencing** of TARGET-WT tumors (GRCh38);
- `TARGET_WT_clinical.tsv`: one row per tumor sample, with the patient's histology, age, sex and vital status.

```{r load-maf, echo=TRUE}
maf_table <- read_tsv("data/somatic/TARGET_WT_somatic_mutations.maf.gz",
                      col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))
clinical  <- read_tsv("data/somatic/TARGET_WT_clinical.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{r table-maf-columns}
kable(
  tribble(
    ~column, ~meaning,
    "Hugo_Symbol", "Gene",
    "Chromosome, Start_Position", "Where the mutation is",
    "Reference_Allele, Tumor_Seq_Allele2", "Normal and mutated base(s)",
    "Variant_Classification", "Consequence: Missense_Mutation, Nonsense_Mutation, Frame_Shift_Del, Splice_Site...",
    "HGVSp_Short", "Protein change, e.g. p.R248Q",
    "Tumor_Sample_Barcode", "Which tumor sample",
    "t_alt_count, t_depth", "Reads supporting the mutation / total reads in the tumor"
  ),
  caption = "The MAF columns used in this module (the file has many more)."
)
```

```{r table-maf-preview}
datatable(
  maf_table %>%
    select(Hugo_Symbol, Chromosome, Start_Position, Reference_Allele, Tumor_Seq_Allele2,
           Variant_Classification, HGVSp_Short, Tumor_Sample_Barcode, t_alt_count, t_depth),
  extensions = "Buttons",
  options = list(dom = "Bfrtip", buttons = c("csv", "excel"), pageLength = 8, scrollX = TRUE),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = "The somatic mutations, one row per mutation."
)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**How few mutations!** The whole file has `r nrow(maf_table)` mutations for `r n_distinct(maf_table$Tumor_Sample_Barcode)` tumor samples, a handful per tumor. Pediatric cancers have far fewer mutations than adult ones: they arise in a few years rather than decades, without the accumulated damage of aging, smoking or UV light. Part 4 puts a number on this.
</div>

The **variant allele fraction** (VAF = `t_alt_count / t_depth`) is the fraction of tumor reads carrying the mutation. A heterozygous mutation present in every tumor cell of a pure sample has VAF ≈ 0.5; normal cells mixed into the sample, or a mutation present only in a subclone, lower it.

```{r plot-vaf, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
maf_table %>%
  mutate(vaf = as.numeric(t_alt_count) / as.numeric(t_depth)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = vaf)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.025, fill = "#8e44ad", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Variant allele fraction (VAF)", y = "Mutations", title = "VAF of all somatic mutations") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)
```

# Part 2 — One Sample per Patient

The TARGET barcode tells us more than the patient: `TARGET-50-PAJLKR-01A-01D` = program, disease code (50 = Wilms tumor), **patient**, **sample type** (01 = primary tumor, 02 = recurrent tumor), vial, portion and analyte (D = DNA).

```{r barcodes, echo=TRUE}
samples <- clinical %>%
  mutate(sample_type = if_else(str_sub(word(Tumor_Sample_Barcode, 4, sep = "-"), 1, 2) == "01",
                               "Primary", "Recurrent"))

samples_per_patient <- samples %>% group_by(case_submitter_id) %>% filter(n() > 1) %>% ungroup()
```

```{r table-duplicates}
kable(samples_per_patient %>% select(case_submitter_id, Tumor_Sample_Barcode, sample_type, histologic_subtype),
      caption = "Patients with more than one sequenced tumor sample.")
```

Some patients contribute both a **primary** and a **recurrent** tumor. For cohort statistics ("how many *patients* carry a TP53 mutation?") each patient must count once, otherwise those patients would weigh double. We keep **one sample per patient**: the primary tumor when available.

```{r one-per-patient, echo=TRUE}
cohort <- samples %>%
  arrange(case_submitter_id, sample_type != "Primary") %>%
  distinct(case_submitter_id, .keep_all = TRUE)

maf <- read.maf(
  maf          = maf_table %>% filter(Tumor_Sample_Barcode %in% cohort$Tumor_Sample_Barcode),
  clinicalData = cohort,
  verbose      = FALSE
)
maf
```

```{r table-cohort}
kable(count(cohort, histologic_subtype, name = "patients"), caption = "Patients in the analysis, by histology.")
```

# Part 3 — Cohort Summary

`plotmafSummary()` gives the overview of a cohort in one figure: mutations per sample, their types, and the most frequently mutated genes.

```{r plot-maf-summary, fig.width=11, fig.height=7}
plotmafSummary(maf, rmOutlier = TRUE, addStat = "median", dashboard = TRUE, titvRaw = FALSE)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**How to read it.** *Variant Classification*: missense mutations dominate, as in almost every cancer. *Variants per sample*: the red line is the median, a few mutations per exome. *Top 10 mutated genes*: the percentage is the fraction of patients with at least one mutation in that gene.
</div>

# Part 4 — Tumor Mutational Burden

**Tumor mutational burden (TMB)** is the number of somatic mutations per **megabase** of sequenced DNA. It matters clinically: tumors with very high TMB (e.g. melanoma, lung cancer in smokers) respond better to immunotherapy, because more mutations mean more abnormal proteins the immune system can recognize.

```{r tmb, echo=TRUE}
# Exome capture kits target roughly 35-50 Mb; maftools needs the size to turn counts into a rate.
tmb_table <- tmb(maf, captureSize = 50, logScale = TRUE)
```

```{r table-tmb}
kable(
  tmb_table %>% as_tibble() %>%
    summarise(patients = n(), median_mutations = median(total), median_TMB_per_Mb = round(median(total_perMB), 3),
              max_TMB_per_Mb = round(max(total_perMB), 3)),
  caption = "TMB in TARGET-WT (mutations per Mb, assuming a 50 Mb exome)."
)
```

How does that compare with adult cancers? `tcgaCompare()` places our cohort among the 33 adult cancer types of **TCGA** (data bundled with maftools):

```{r plot-tcga-compare, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}
tcga_comparison <- tcgaCompare(maf, cohortName = "TARGET-WT", capture_size = 50, logscale = TRUE)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Wilms tumor sits at the far left, below every adult cancer type**, even the lowest-burden ones (acute myeloid leukemia, pheochromocytoma, thyroid cancer), and roughly 80 times below melanoma. Low TMB is typical of pediatric cancers, which are driven by a few key genetic events (or by epigenetic changes, such as the 11p15.5 imprinting defects of Module 1's region) rather than by thousands of mutations. It is also one reason immunotherapy has so far had limited success in most childhood solid tumors.
</div>

## Transitions and Transversions

The kind of base change carries a memory of what caused it. `titv()` classifies every SNV into the six possible substitution types.

```{r plot-titv, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
titv_result <- titv(maf, plot = FALSE, useSyn = TRUE)
plotTiTv(titv_result)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**C>T dominates.** The most frequent change in almost every tumor is C>T, largely due to the spontaneous deamination of methylated cytosines (5-methylcytosine → thymine), a "clock-like" process that accumulates slowly with every cell division. Specific exposures leave different marks (e.g. C>A for tobacco smoke, C>T at dipyrimidines for UV light); a formal **mutational signature** analysis needs many more mutations per tumor than Wilms tumors carry.
</div>

# Part 5 — The Mutated Genes

An **oncoplot** is the standard picture of a cancer cohort: one column per patient, one row per gene, colored by the type of mutation. The bar on top shows each patient's number of mutations; the annotation below, the histology.

```{r plot-oncoplot-top, fig.width=11, fig.height=7}
histology_colors <- list(histologic_subtype = c(Favorable = "#2980b9", Unfavorable = "#e74c3c"))

oncoplot(maf, top = 15, clinicalFeatures = "histologic_subtype", annotationColor = histology_colors,
         sortByAnnotation = TRUE, removeNonMutated = FALSE, fontSize = 0.7, showTumorSampleBarcodes = FALSE)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Frequent is not the same as important.** `TP53` is a real cancer gene. But `TTN` (titin, the largest human protein) and other very long genes appear near the top of almost every cancer cohort simply because they offer the biggest target to random mutations. Telling **drivers** (mutations that give the cell an advantage) from **passengers** (neutral hitchhikers) needs more than counting: prior knowledge, recurrence at the same position, or statistical models of the background mutation rate.
</div>

## Known Wilms Tumor Drivers

Wilms tumor has a well-studied set of driver genes, falling into a few pathways: the **WT1/β-catenin** pathway (`WT1`, `CTNNB1`, `AMER1`), **microRNA processing** (`DROSHA`, `DGCR8`, `DICER1`), **kidney development** transcription factors (`SIX1`, `SIX2`), **chromatin and transcription regulators** (`MLLT1`, `BCOR`, `ARID1A`, `CDC73`), and `TP53` in anaplastic tumors.

```{r drivers, echo=TRUE}
wilms_drivers <- c("TP53", "WT1", "CTNNB1", "AMER1", "DROSHA", "DGCR8", "DICER1",
                   "SIX1", "SIX2", "MYCN", "MLLT1", "BCOR", "ARID1A", "CDC73")
drivers_found <- intersect(wilms_drivers, getGeneSummary(maf)$Hugo_Symbol)
```

```{r plot-oncoplot-drivers, fig.width=11, fig.height=5.5}
oncoplot(maf, genes = drivers_found, clinicalFeatures = "histologic_subtype", annotationColor = histology_colors,
         sortByAnnotation = TRUE, removeNonMutated = FALSE, keepGeneOrder = TRUE,
         fontSize = 0.8, showTumorSampleBarcodes = FALSE)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Most patients carry no known driver mutation in this list.** Several reasons add up: many Wilms tumors are driven by **non-mutational** events (loss of imprinting at 11p15.5, deletions of whole regions such as `WT1`, copy-number changes) that a mutation list cannot show; `AMER1` deletions and some `WT1` alterations are large deletions, not point mutations; and the **masked open-access** MAF removes calls supported by a single caller or failing quality filters. Absence from a MAF is not proof of a normal gene.
</div>

# Part 6 — TP53 in Detail

A **lollipop plot** places each mutation on the protein, over its functional domains. The height of a lollipop is the number of patients with that mutation.

```{r plot-lollipop, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.5}
lollipopPlot(maf, gene = "TP53", AACol = "HGVSp_Short", showMutationRate = TRUE, labelPos = "all",
             labPosSize = 0.8, printCount = TRUE)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Mutations cluster in the DNA-binding domain.** p53 is a transcription factor that halts the cell cycle or triggers death after DNA damage. Almost all cancer mutations hit its **DNA-binding domain**, often at the same "hotspot" residues (R175, R248, R273...), destroying its ability to bind its target genes. Clustering at recurrent positions is one of the strongest signs that a gene is a real driver rather than a passenger.
</div>

```{r table-tp53}
datatable(
  subsetMaf(maf, genes = "TP53", mafObj = FALSE) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    left_join(cohort %>% select(Tumor_Sample_Barcode, histologic_subtype), by = "Tumor_Sample_Barcode") %>%
    transmute(Tumor_Sample_Barcode, histologic_subtype, Variant_Classification, HGVSp_Short,
              VAF = round(as.numeric(t_alt_count) / as.numeric(t_depth), 2)),
  rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "tp", pageLength = 15),
  caption = "Every TP53 mutation in the cohort."
)
```

# Part 7 — Favorable vs Unfavorable Histology

Do the two histologies carry different mutations? `clinicalEnrichment()` tests, for every gene mutated in at least a few patients, whether it is mutated more often in one group than in the others (**Fisher's exact test**).

```{r clinical-enrichment, echo=TRUE}
enrichment <- clinicalEnrichment(maf, clinicalFeature = "histologic_subtype", minMut = 3)
```

```{r table-enrichment}
kable(
  enrichment$groupwise_comparision %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    filter(Group1 == "Unfavorable") %>%
    transmute(gene = Hugo_Symbol, `mutated in Unfavorable` = n_mutated_group1, `mutated in Favorable` = n_mutated_group2,
              p_value = signif(p_value, 3), fdr = signif(fdr, 3)),
  caption = "Genes mutated in at least 3 patients: Unfavorable vs Favorable."
)
```

```{r plot-enrichment, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
plotEnrichmentResults(enrich_res = enrichment, pVal = 0.05, geneFontSize = 0.8, annoFontSize = 0.7)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**TP53 is the defining mutation of anaplastic Wilms tumor.** Anaplasia, the histological hallmark of the Unfavorable group (large, abnormal nuclei and chaotic mitoses), is tightly linked to loss of p53: without it, cells with damaged or abnormal genomes are no longer stopped. This is why TP53 status is studied as a biomarker for risk stratification: it identifies the tumors most likely to resist standard therapy. The result here, obtained from a few dozen exomes, reproduces one of the best-established findings in Wilms tumor biology.

**A caution on small numbers.** With `r nrow(cohort)` patients only very strong differences can reach significance. Genes mutated in 1–2 patients cannot be tested meaningfully at all, which is the normal situation in pediatric cancer genomics: findings need large, multi-center cohorts to be confirmed.
</div>

# Summary

- **Germline** variants are inherited and in every cell; **somatic** mutations are acquired by the tumor and found by comparing tumor and normal DNA.
- A **MAF** lists somatic mutations with their annotation; **one sample per patient** must be kept for cohort statistics.
- Wilms tumor has a **very low mutational burden**, typical of pediatric cancers.
- Frequent genes are not necessarily drivers: **TP53**, with mutations clustered in its DNA-binding domain, is a true driver, and it is **specific to Unfavorable (anaplastic) histology**.
